sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Show that \(f(x)=x^3-4x-2\) has a root between \(x=2\) and \(x=3\).
questions.target: Locating roots by a change of sign
questions.answer: \(f(2)=8-8-2=-2\). \(f(3)=27-12-2=13\). Since \(f(2)<0\) and \(f(3)>0\), the sign change confirms a root lies in \((2,3)\).
questions.explanation: \(f(2)=8-8-2=-2\). \(f(3)=27-12-2=13\). Since \(f(2)<0\) and \(f(3)>0\), the sign change confirms a root lies in \((2,3)\).

questions.q: Using \(f(x)=x^3-x-1\), which changes sign between \(x=1\) and \(x=2\), evaluate \(f(1.5)\) and give a narrower interval containing the root.
Continuing from the previous problem, evaluate \(f(1.25)\) and give a narrower interval for the root.
Using \(f(x)=\ln x-2+x\), which changes sign between \(x=1\) and \(x=2\), evaluate \(f(1.5)\) and give a narrower interval for the root.
The equation \(x^3-4x-2=0\) rearranges to \(x=\sqrt[3]{4x+2}\). Using \(x_0=2\), find \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and \(x_3\), to four decimal places.
Explain why the iteration \(x_{n+1}=x_n^3-3\) (i.e. \(g(x)=x^3-3\)), starting from \(x_0=1.5\), would fail to converge to a root of \(x^3-x-3=0\) near \(x=1.5\).
questions.answer: \(g'(x)=3x^2\). At \(x=1.5\): \(g'(1.5)=3(2.25)=6.75\). Since \(|g'(1.5)|=6.75>1\), the iteration does not satisfy the convergence condition \(|g'(x)|<1\) near this point, so it diverges rather than converging to the root.
questions.explanation: \(g'(x)=3x^2\). At \(x=1.5\): \(g'(1.5)=3(2.25)=6.75\). Since \(|g'(1.5)|=6.75>1\), the iteration does not satisfy the convergence condition \(|g'(x)|<1\) near this point, so it diverges rather than converging to the root.

questions.q: Using \(g(x)=5-\frac{2}{x}\) from the earlier iteration, find \(g'(x)\) and evaluate \(|g'(x)|\) at \(x=4.56\) (near the root), to explain why the iteration converges there.
questions.answer: \(g(x)=5-2x^{-1}\), so \(g'(x)=\frac{2}{x^2}\). At \(x=4.56\): \(g'(4.56)=\frac{2}{20.7936}\approx0.0962\). Since \(|g'(4.56)|<1\), the iteration converges near this root.
questions.explanation: \(g(x)=5-2x^{-1}\), so \(g'(x)=\frac{2}{x^2}\). At \(x=4.56\): \(g'(4.56)=\frac{2}{20.7936}\approx0.0962\). Since \(|g'(4.56)|<1\), the iteration converges near this root.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Rearrange \(x^2-3x-1=0\) into the form \(x=g(x)\) by making the linear term the subject.
Rearrange \(x^3+x-1=0\) into the form \(x=\frac{1}{x^2+1}\), and verify algebraically that this is equivalent to the original equation.
questions.answer: From \(x^3+x-1=0\): \(x(x^2+1)=1\), so \(x=\frac{1}{x^2+1}\). Verifying: multiplying both sides by \((x^2+1)\) gives \(x(x^2+1)=1\), i.e. \(x^3+x=1\), i.e. \(x^3+x-1=0\), which matches the original equation exactly.
questions.explanation: From \(x^3+x-1=0\): \(x(x^2+1)=1\), so \(x=\frac{1}{x^2+1}\). Verifying: multiplying both sides by \((x^2+1)\) gives \(x(x^2+1)=1\), i.e. \(x^3+x=1\), i.e. \(x^3+x-1=0\), which matches the original equation exactly.

questions.q: Use one iteration of the Newton-Raphson method, \(x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\), with \(x_0=2\) to find \(x_1\) for \(f(x)=x^3-4x-2\), to four decimal places.
Continuing from \(x_1=2.25\) in the previous problem, find \(x_2\), to four decimal places.
Use the Newton-Raphson method with \(x_0=2.5\) to find \(x_1\) for \(f(x)=x^2-7\) (approximating \(\sqrt{7}\)), to four decimal places.
Use the Newton-Raphson method with \(x_0=2\) to find \(x_1\) for \(f(x)=x^3-2x-5\), to four decimal places.
Using \(x_1=2.65\) from the previous problem for \(f(x)=x^2-7\), perform a second iteration to find \(x_2\), to four decimal places, and compare with \(\sqrt{7}\approx2.6458\).
questions.target: Further Newton-Raphson: rapid convergence and failure cases
questions.answer: \(f(2.65)=7.0225-7=0.0225\). \(f'(2.65)=5.3\). \(x_2=2.65-\frac{0.0225}{5.3}\approx2.65-0.00425\approx2.6458\), matching \(\sqrt{7}\) to four decimal places after just two iterations.
questions.explanation: \(f(2.65)=7.0225-7=0.0225\). \(f'(2.65)=5.3\). \(x_2=2.65-\frac{0.0225}{5.3}\approx2.65-0.00425\approx2.6458\), matching \(\sqrt{7}\) to four decimal places after just two iterations.

questions.q: Explain why \(x_0=1\) is an unsuitable starting point for the Newton-Raphson method applied to \(f(x)=x^3-3x+1\).
questions.target: Further Newton-Raphson: rapid convergence and failure cases
questions.answer: \(f'(x)=3x^2-3\). At \(x_0=1\): \(f'(1)=3-3=0\). Since \(f'(1)=0\), the tangent line at \(x_0=1\) is horizontal and never meets the \(x\)-axis, so the formula \(x_1=x_0-\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\) involves division by zero — the method fails at this starting point.
questions.explanation: \(f'(x)=3x^2-3\). At \(x_0=1\): \(f'(1)=3-3=0\). Since \(f'(1)=0\), the tangent line at \(x_0=1\) is horizontal and never meets the \(x\)-axis, so the formula \(x_1=x_0-\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\) involves division by zero — the method fails at this starting point.

questions.q: An interval of width 32 containing a root must be reduced to width at most 1 using repeated bisection. Find the minimum number of bisections required.
questions.answer: Halving repeatedly, after \(n\) bisections the width is \(32/2^n\). The smallest \(n\) with \(32/2^n\leq 1\) is \(n=5\) (width becomes \(1\)).
questions.explanation: Halving repeatedly, after \(n\) bisections the width is \(32/2^n\). The smallest \(n\) with \(32/2^n\leq 1\) is \(n=5\) (width becomes \(1\)).

questions.q: An interval of width 8 containing a root is bisected 3 times. Find the width of the resulting interval.
questions.answer: Each bisection halves the width: \(\frac{8}{2^{3}}=1\).

questions.q: Using the Newton-Raphson method with \( f(x)=x^2-18 \) and \( x_0=5 \), find \( x_1 \).
The continuous function \(f\) is defined for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x) = 2^x + 3x - 11.\) Between which pair of consecutive integers does a root of the equation \(f(x) = 0\) lie?
questions.answer: To determine the interval containing a root of a continuous function \(f(x)\), we use the change-of-sign rule (Intermediate Value Theorem). If \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, then at least one real root of \(f(x) = 0\) lies in the interval \((a, b)\). Evaluate \(f(x)\) at consecutive integers: - For \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 2^0 + 3(0) - 11 = 1 + 0 - 11 = -10 0\) - For \(x = 4\): \(f(4) = 2^4 + 3(4) - 11 = 16 + 12 - 11 = 17 > 0\) Since \(f(2) = -1 0\), there is a change of sign between \(x = 2\) and \(x = 3\). Because \(f\) is continuous, a root of \(f(x) = 0\) lies between \(2\) and \(3\). Common misconception: In the interval \([1, 2]\), \(f(1) = -6\) and \(f(2) = -1\). Although the value increases significantly, both values remain negative, so no root is guaranteed in \([1, 2]\).
questions.explanation: To determine the interval containing a root of a continuous function \(f(x)\), we use the change-of-sign rule (Intermediate Value Theorem). If \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, then at least one real root of \(f(x) = 0\) lies in the interval \((a, b)\). Evaluate \(f(x)\) at consecutive integers: - For \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 2^0 + 3(0) - 11 = 1 + 0 - 11 = -10 0\) - For \(x = 4\): \(f(4) = 2^4 + 3(4) - 11 = 16 + 12 - 11 = 17 > 0\) Since \(f(2) = -1 0\), there is a change of sign between \(x = 2\) and \(x = 3\). Because \(f\) is continuous, a root of \(f(x) = 0\) lies between \(2\) and \(3\). Common misconception: In the interval \([1, 2]\), \(f(1) = -6\) and \(f(2) = -1\). Although the value increases significantly, both values remain negative, so no root is guaranteed in \([1, 2]\).

questions.q: A confidence interval for the mean uses \(z=1\), \(\sigma=4\), \(n=9\). Find the margin of error \(E=z\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).
questions.target: Further Newton-Raphson: rapid convergence and failure cases
questions.answer: Applying Sampling & Estimation principles, \(E=1\times4/3=\frac{4}{3}\). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(\frac{4}{3}\).
questions.explanation: Applying Sampling & Estimation principles, \(E=1\times4/3=\frac{4}{3}\). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(\frac{4}{3}\).

questions.q: Which differential equation correctly models the statement: "The rate of increase of the number of infected people N is proportional to the product of N and the number of remaining susceptible people \((S-N)\), for fixed population S."?
questions.answer: The correct model is \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN(S-N)\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.
questions.explanation: The correct model is \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN(S-N)\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.

questions.q: The curve \(C\) has equation \(y = \frac{\ln x}{x^2}, \quad x > 0.\) The point \(M\) is the stationary point of \(C\), and the line \(L\) is the tangent to \(C\) at \(M\). The finite region \(R\) is bounded by the curve \(C\), the tangent line \(L\), and the vertical line \(x = 1\). Find the exact area of \(R\).
questions.answer: 1. **Find the stationary point \(M\):** Using the quotient rule to differentiate \(y = \frac{\ln x}{x^2}\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{1}{x} \cdot x^2 - (\ln x)(2x)}{x^4} = \frac{x(1 - 2\ln x)}{x^4} = \frac{1 - 2\ln x}{x^3}.\) Setting \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\): $1 - 2\ln x = 0 \Rightarrow \ln x = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = e^{1/2} = \sqrt{e}.\( The \)y\(-coordinate at \)M\( is: \)y = \frac{\ln(\sqrt{e})}{(\sqrt{e})^2} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{e} = \frac{1}{2e}.\( Since \)M\( is a stationary point, the tangent line \)L\( is horizontal with equation \)y = \frac{1}{2e}\(. 2. **Set up the integral for the area:** For \)1 \leq x \leq \sqrt{e}\(, the tangent line \)L\( lies above the curve \)C\(. The region \)R\( is bounded on the left by \)x = 1\( and on the right by \)x = \sqrt{e}\( where \)C\( touches \)L\(: \)\mathrm{Area} = \int_{1}^{\sqrt{e}} \left( \frac{1}{2e} - \frac{\ln x}{x^2} \right) dx.\( 3. **Integrate \)\int \frac{\ln x}{x^2} \, dx\( by parts:** Let \)u = \ln x \Rightarrow du = \frac{1}{x} \, dx\(, and \)dv = x^{-2} \, dx \Rightarrow v = -\frac{1}{x}\(. \)\int \frac{\ln x}{x^2} \, dx = -\frac{\ln x}{x} - \int \left(-\frac{1}{x^2}\right) dx = -\frac{\ln x}{x} - \frac{1}{x} = -\frac{\ln x + 1}{x}.\( Thus, the antiderivative of the integrand is: \)F(x) = \frac{x}{2e} + \frac{\ln x + 1}{x}.\( 4. **Evaluate between limits \)1\( and \)\sqrt{e}\(:** At \)x = \sqrt{e}\(: \)F(\sqrt{e}) = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2e} + \frac{\frac{1}{2} + 1}{\sqrt{e}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{e}} + \frac{3}{2\sqrt{e}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{e}} = \frac{4\sqrt{e}}{2e}.\( At \)x = 1\(: \)F(1) = \frac{1}{2e} + \frac{0 + 1}{1} = \frac{1}{2e} + 1 = \frac{2e + 1}{2e}.\( Subtracting the two values: \)\mathrm{Area} = F(\sqrt{e}) - F(1) = \frac{4\sqrt{e}}{2e} - \frac{2e + 1}{2e} = \frac{4\sqrt{e} - 2e - 1}{2e}.$
questions.explanation: 1. **Find the stationary point \(M\):** Using the quotient rule to differentiate \(y = \frac{\ln x}{x^2}\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{1}{x} \cdot x^2 - (\ln x)(2x)}{x^4} = \frac{x(1 - 2\ln x)}{x^4} = \frac{1 - 2\ln x}{x^3}.\) Setting \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\): $1 - 2\ln x = 0 \Rightarrow \ln x = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = e^{1/2} = \sqrt{e}.\( The \)y\(-coordinate at \)M\( is: \)y = \frac{\ln(\sqrt{e})}{(\sqrt{e})^2} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{e} = \frac{1}{2e}.\( Since \)M\( is a stationary point, the tangent line \)L\( is horizontal with equation \)y = \frac{1}{2e}\(. 2. **Set up the integral for the area:** For \)1 \leq x \leq \sqrt{e}\(, the tangent line \)L\( lies above the curve \)C\(. The region \)R\( is bounded on the left by \)x = 1\( and on the right by \)x = \sqrt{e}\( where \)C\( touches \)L\(: \)\mathrm{Area} = \int_{1}^{\sqrt{e}} \left( \frac{1}{2e} - \frac{\ln x}{x^2} \right) dx.\( 3. **Integrate \)\int \frac{\ln x}{x^2} \, dx\( by parts:** Let \)u = \ln x \Rightarrow du = \frac{1}{x} \, dx\(, and \)dv = x^{-2} \, dx \Rightarrow v = -\frac{1}{x}\(. \)\int \frac{\ln x}{x^2} \, dx = -\frac{\ln x}{x} - \int \left(-\frac{1}{x^2}\right) dx = -\frac{\ln x}{x} - \frac{1}{x} = -\frac{\ln x + 1}{x}.\( Thus, the antiderivative of the integrand is: \)F(x) = \frac{x}{2e} + \frac{\ln x + 1}{x}.\( 4. **Evaluate between limits \)1\( and \)\sqrt{e}\(:** At \)x = \sqrt{e}\(: \)F(\sqrt{e}) = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2e} + \frac{\frac{1}{2} + 1}{\sqrt{e}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{e}} + \frac{3}{2\sqrt{e}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{e}} = \frac{4\sqrt{e}}{2e}.\( At \)x = 1\(: \)F(1) = \frac{1}{2e} + \frac{0 + 1}{1} = \frac{1}{2e} + 1 = \frac{2e + 1}{2e}.\( Subtracting the two values: \)\mathrm{Area} = F(\sqrt{e}) - F(1) = \frac{4\sqrt{e}}{2e} - \frac{2e + 1}{2e} = \frac{4\sqrt{e} - 2e - 1}{2e}.$

questions.q: Using the Newton-Raphson method with \( f(x)=x^2-13 \) and \( x_0=2 \), find \( x_1 \).
A curve has equation \(y = x^2 e^{3x}\). Find the gradient of the curve at the point where \(x = 1\).
questions.answer: To find the gradient of the curve, differentiate \(y = x^2 e^{3x}\) with respect to \(x\) using the product rule: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}[u v] = u \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} + v \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}\) Let \(u = x^2\) and \(v = e^{3x}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2x\) and, by the chain rule, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3e^{3x}\). Applying the product rule: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = x^2(3e^{3x}) + 2x(e^{3x}) = (3x^2 + 2x)e^{3x}\) Substitute \(x = 1\): \(\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \right|_{x=1} = (3(1)^2 + 2(1))e^{3(1)} = (3 + 2)e^3 = 5e^3\) Common misconceptions: - \(6e^3\) arises from mistakenly differentiating a product by multiplying the individual derivatives: \((2x)(3e^{3x}) = 6x e^{3x} \rightarrow 6e^3\). - \(3e^3\) arises from forgetting the chain rule factor when differentiating \(e^{3x}\), treating \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^{3x})\) as \(e^{3x}\). - \(2e^3\) arises from differentiating only \(x^2\) while treating \(e^{3x}\) as a constant.
questions.explanation: To find the gradient of the curve, differentiate \(y = x^2 e^{3x}\) with respect to \(x\) using the product rule: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}[u v] = u \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} + v \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}\) Let \(u = x^2\) and \(v = e^{3x}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2x\) and, by the chain rule, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3e^{3x}\). Applying the product rule: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = x^2(3e^{3x}) + 2x(e^{3x}) = (3x^2 + 2x)e^{3x}\) Substitute \(x = 1\): \(\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \right|_{x=1} = (3(1)^2 + 2(1))e^{3(1)} = (3 + 2)e^3 = 5e^3\) Common misconceptions: - \(6e^3\) arises from mistakenly differentiating a product by multiplying the individual derivatives: \((2x)(3e^{3x}) = 6x e^{3x} \rightarrow 6e^3\). - \(3e^3\) arises from forgetting the chain rule factor when differentiating \(e^{3x}\), treating \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^{3x})\) as \(e^{3x}\). - \(2e^3\) arises from differentiating only \(x^2\) while treating \(e^{3x}\) as a constant.

questions.q: An interval of width 32 containing a root must be reduced to width at most 2 using repeated bisection. Find the minimum number of bisections required.
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. Halving repeatedly, after \( n \) bisections the width is \( 32/2^n \). The smallest \( n \) with \( 32/2^n\le 2 \) is \( n=4 \) (width becomes \( 2 \)). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: Halving repeatedly, after \( n \) bisections the width is \( 32/2^n \). The smallest \( n \) with \( 32/2^n\le 2 \) is \( n=4 \) (width becomes \( 2 \)). [M1][A1]

questions.q: Relative to a fixed origin \(O\), the points \(A\) and \(B\) have position vectors \(\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \overrightarrow{OB} = 3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}.\) Find the length of the vector \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
questions.target: Locating roots by a change of sign
questions.answer: To find the vector \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), subtract the position vector of \(A\) from that of \(B\): \(\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OB} - \overrightarrow{OA} = (3 - 1)\mathbf{i} + (2 - 5)\mathbf{j} + (4 - (-2))\mathbf{k} = 2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}.\) The magnitude (length) of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is: \(|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7.\) Common misconceptions: - Incorrectly taking \((-3)^2 = -9\) leads to \(\sqrt{4 - 9 + 36} = \sqrt{31}\). - Adding the position vectors instead of subtracting yields \(\sqrt{4^2 + 7^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{69}\). - Forgetting to take the square root gives \(49\).

questions.q: Find the particular solution of the differential equation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2x e^{-y}\) given that \(y = 0\) when \(x = 0\).
questions.answer: To solve the differential equation, we use separation of variables: 1. **Separate the variables**: \(e^y \,\mathrm{d}y = 2x \,\mathrm{d}x\) 2. **Integrate both sides**: \(\int e^y \,\mathrm{d}y = \int 2x \,\mathrm{d}x\) \(e^y = x^2 + C\) 3. **Apply the initial condition** \(y = 0\) when \(x = 0\): \(e^0 = 0^2 + C \Rightarrow 1 = C\) *(A frequent error is assuming \(C = 0\) because the boundary values are zero, which leads to the incorrect solution \(y = \ln(x^2)\).)* 4. **Express \(y\) explicitly in terms of \(x\)**: \(e^y = x^2 + 1 \Rightarrow y = \ln(x^2 + 1)\) Thus, the correct choice is \(y = \ln(x^2 + 1)\).
questions.explanation: To solve the differential equation, we use separation of variables: 1. **Separate the variables**: \(e^y \,\mathrm{d}y = 2x \,\mathrm{d}x\) 2. **Integrate both sides**: \(\int e^y \,\mathrm{d}y = \int 2x \,\mathrm{d}x\) \(e^y = x^2 + C\) 3. **Apply the initial condition** \(y = 0\) when \(x = 0\): \(e^0 = 0^2 + C \Rightarrow 1 = C\) *(A frequent error is assuming \(C = 0\) because the boundary values are zero, which leads to the incorrect solution \(y = \ln(x^2)\).)* 4. **Express \(y\) explicitly in terms of \(x\)**: \(e^y = x^2 + 1 \Rightarrow y = \ln(x^2 + 1)\) Thus, the correct choice is \(y = \ln(x^2 + 1)\).

A curve satisfies \(x^2+y^2=25\). Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at the point \((3,-4)\).
questions.answer: Differentiating implicitly: \(2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}\). At \((3,-4)\): \(\frac{3}{4}\).
questions.explanation: Differentiating implicitly: \(2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}\). At \((3,-4)\): \(\frac{3}{4}\).

questions.q: Which differential equation correctly models the statement: "The rate of decrease of the temperature T of an object is proportional to the difference between T and the surrounding temperature \(T_e\)."?
questions.answer: The correct model is \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_e)\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.
questions.explanation: The correct model is \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_e)\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.

questions.q: Which differential equation correctly models the statement: "The rate of increase of the volume V of a balloon is proportional to the square of its radius r."?
questions.answer: The correct model is \(\frac{dV}{dt}=kr^2\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.
questions.explanation: The correct model is \(\frac{dV}{dt}=kr^2\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.

questions.q: Which differential equation correctly models the statement: "The rate of decrease of a radioactive mass m is proportional to m."?
questions.target: Further Newton-Raphson: rapid convergence and failure cases
questions.answer: The correct model is \(\frac{dm}{dt}=-km\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.
questions.explanation: The correct model is \(\frac{dm}{dt}=-km\), where \(k>0\) is a constant of proportionality.
